blocks.content: The reliability in TCP topic introduced sequence numbers at a conceptual, big picture level, just enough to know they exist and roughly why. This topic delivers the exact mechanics: precisely what gets numbered, how the numbering actually works, and what happens at the edges, gaps and wraparound included.

Get this one detail right and a huge amount of TCP behavior suddenly makes sense. Get it wrong, and reordering, loss detection, and acknowledgment all stay confusing. So start here, with the single most important fact about TCP sequence numbers.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014434302-185718114.png
blocks.alt: TCP numbers every individual byte of the data stream, not the segments and not the packets carrying them

blocks.content: 1. The Crucial Detail: Sequence Numbers Count Bytes, Not Segments
blocks.text: 1. The Crucial Detail: Sequence Numbers Count Bytes, Not Segments

blocks.content: This is genuinely the single most common point of confusion worth stating plainly up front. TCP does not number the segments themselves, it numbers every single individual byte of data in the stream. If a segment carries 500 bytes of data starting at sequence number 1000, that segment covers bytes numbered 1000 through 1499, and the very next segment sent will start at sequence number 1500.

blocks.title: Say it once more, clearly
blocks.content: A sequence number identifies a specific byte position in the stream, not a specific segment. This one fact underlies almost everything else in this topic.
2. A Worked Example, Byte by Byte
blocks.text: 2. A Worked Example, Byte by Byte

blocks.content: Starting sequence number 1000. The first segment carries 500 bytes, covering bytes 1000 through 1499. The second segment carries 300 bytes, covering 1500 through 1799. The third segment carries 200 bytes, covering 1800 through 1999. Notice each segment can be a genuinely different size, and the numbering still lines up perfectly, since every byte, not every segment, gets its own number.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014436732-242208419.png
blocks.alt: Three segments of different sizes, each covering an exact, non overlapping range of byte numbers

blocks.content: 3. Why Counting Bytes Instead of Segments Genuinely Matters
blocks.text: 3. Why Counting Bytes Instead of Segments Genuinely Matters

blocks.content: If a segment gets lost and needs to be resent, TCP does not need to guess where it fell in some segment counting scheme, it knows exactly, by byte number, precisely what data is missing and needs to be resent. This also means segments of completely different sizes are handled completely naturally, with no special casing needed anywhere.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014438392-620292730.png
blocks.alt: Byte level numbering means TCP knows exactly what data is missing, regardless of how segments happened to be sized

blocks.content: 4. Connecting Back to the Handshake

Recall from the three way handshake topic that each side picks its own random starting sequence number during connection setup. Every subsequent sequence number for that direction of the connection is simply an offset counted forward from that random starting point, not counted from zero.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014439946-460542897.png
blocks.alt: Every byte after the handshake is numbered as an offset forward from that connection random starting point

blocks.content: 5. Sequence Number Wraparound

Sequence numbers are stored in a fixed size field and cannot grow forever. Once a connection has transferred enough data that the count would exceed the maximum representable value, it wraps back around to zero and continues counting from there. This is a real thing that happens on any sufficiently long lived, high volume connection, not a hypothetical edge case invented for a textbook.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014441479-257932623.png
blocks.alt: Sequence numbers wrap back around to zero once they hit the maximum value the field can hold, on any long enough connection

blocks.title: Not a rare edge case
blocks.content: Wraparound sounds exotic but it genuinely happens on real, long lived, high throughput connections. TCP implementations handle it correctly by design, it is not something applications need to worry about themselves.
6. How the Receiver Detects Gaps and Duplicates
blocks.text: 6. How the Receiver Detects Gaps and Duplicates

blocks.content: The receiver tracks exactly which byte number it expects next. If a segment arrives with a HIGHER sequence number than expected, the receiver knows something in between is missing and has not arrived yet. If a segment arrives with a sequence number the receiver has already seen, it recognizes this as a duplicate and simply discards it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014443210-461608798.png
blocks.alt: The receiver compares an arriving segment number against what it expects next, revealing gaps or duplicates immediately

blocks.content: 7. A Worked Example of Out of Order Arrival
blocks.text: 7. A Worked Example of Out of Order Arrival

blocks.content: Segments covering bytes 1000 to 1499 and 2000 to 2499 arrive, but the segment covering 1500 to 1999 has not arrived yet. The receiver correctly holds onto the out of order data it already has and waits specifically for the missing byte range, reassembling everything in the correct order once that gap finally arrives.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014445062-502489293.png
blocks.alt: Out of order data is held, not discarded, while the receiver waits specifically for the missing byte range to arrive

blocks.content: 8. Bytes Versus a Naive Segment Counting Scheme
blocks.text: 8. Bytes Versus a Naive Segment Counting Scheme

Think of numbered pages in a very long book rather than numbered chapters. If chapters could be any length, referring to a specific missing PAGE number is far more precise and useful than trying to say which fraction of a chapter is missing.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784014447104-800798444.png
blocks.alt: Numbered pages give a precise reference point; numbered chapters of varying length give only a vague one

blocks.content: 9. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming sequence numbers count individual segments or packets, when they actually count individual bytes.","Forgetting that each direction of a connection has its own completely independent sequence numbering, starting from its own separately chosen initial value.","A sequence number identifies a byte position, not a segment.","Segments can be any size, byte counting handles this naturally.","Sequence numbers wrap back to zero on long lived, high volume connections.","Gaps and duplicates are both detected by comparing arriving sequence numbers against what is expected next."]
items: Assuming sequence numbers count individual segments or packets, when they actually count individual bytes.
Forgetting that each direction of a connection has its own completely independent sequence numbering, starting from its own separately chosen initial value.
A sequence number identifies a byte position, not a segment.
Segments can be any size, byte counting handles this naturally.
Sequence numbers wrap back to zero on long lived, high volume connections.
Gaps and duplicates are both detected by comparing arriving sequence numbers against what is expected next.
